lessons.title: Storing many values in a list
lessons.theory_md:
## When one variable per thing stops working

Last week you learned to give a value a name: `price = 2.50`. That works well for one price. It stops working the moment you have thirty.

Imagine writing a program that holds your shopping. With only the tools you have so far you would write `item1 = "milk"`, `item2 = "bread"`, `item3 = "eggs"` — and then what? Add a fourth item and you have to write a new line of code. Ask "how many things am I buying?" and you have to count them by eye. Ask "what was the first thing?" and you have to remember which name you gave it.

Programmers hit this wall very early, and there is a tool for it. It is called a **list**.

## A list is many values, kept in order

A list is one name that holds several values, one after another, in the order you put them in. You write it with square brackets `[ ]` and commas between the values.

```python
shopping = ["milk", "bread", "eggs"]
print(shopping)
print(len(shopping))
```

That prints exactly this:

```
['milk', 'bread', 'eggs']
3
```

Two things happened there. `print(shopping)` showed the whole list, brackets and all — that is how Python writes a list back to you. And `len(shopping)` gave the **length**: how many items are inside. `len` is short for length, and it is one of the words Python already knows.

## Getting one value out: counting starts at zero

To pull a single value out of a list you give its **position** in square brackets. The catch — and it catches everyone — is that Python starts counting at **zero**, not one.

```python
shopping = ["milk", "bread", "eggs"]
print(shopping[0])
print(shopping[1])
print(shopping[2])
print(shopping[-1])
```

Output:

```
milk
bread
eggs
eggs
```

So `shopping[0]` is the first item, `shopping[1]` is the second, and `shopping[2]` is the third. A list of three items has positions 0, 1 and 2 — never 3. The last line shows a shortcut: a negative position counts backwards from the end, so `[-1]` is always the last item, however long the list is.

This zero business is not Python being awkward with you. Think of the position as "how many steps along from the start", and it makes sense: the first item is zero steps from the start.

## Adding and removing

A list can change after you make it. Three instructions cover almost everything a beginner needs.

```python
scores = [12, 7, 20]
scores.append(15)
print(scores)

scores.remove(7)
print(scores)

last = scores.pop()
print(last)
print(scores)
print(len(scores))
```

Output:

```
[12, 7, 20, 15]
[12, 20, 15]
15
[12, 20]
2
```

`append` adds one value to the end. `remove` takes out the first item that matches the **value** you name — you say what it is, not where it is. `pop` takes the last item out and hands it back to you, which is why `last` holds 15. The full stop before each word means "do this to that list"; you will meet that pattern everywhere in Python.

## Starting empty and growing

A list does not have to contain anything when you make it. An empty pair of brackets is a perfectly good list, waiting to be filled.

```python
wins = []
print(len(wins))
wins.append("Tuesday")
wins.append("Thursday")
print(wins)
print(len(wins))
```

Output:

```
0
['Tuesday', 'Thursday']
2
```

This turns out to be one of the most useful patterns in programming. You make an empty list, then add to it as your program works something out. In two lessons time, when you meet loops, you will use it constantly: start empty, look at each thing in turn, keep the ones you want. Get used to the shape of it now.

## The mistakes people actually make here

**Asking for a position that is not there.** This is the classic.

```python
shopping = ["milk", "bread", "eggs"]
print(shopping[3])
```

Python stops and prints:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "shopping.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(shopping[3])
IndexError: list index out of range
```

That block of text is called a traceback, and you will learn to read one properly in week 3. For now read the last line only. `IndexError: list index out of range` means "you asked for a position this list does not have". Three items, positions 0 to 2, and you asked for 3. Nothing is broken and you have done nothing stupid — the message is telling you precisely what it needs.

**Expecting `append` to hand you a new list.** Writing `scores = scores.append(15)` looks reasonable and quietly ruins everything. `append` changes the list where it sits and hands back nothing at all, so `scores` ends up holding nothing. Write `scores.append(15)` on its own line.

**Removing a value that is not in the list.** `shopping.remove("jam")` when there is no jam gives `ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list`. Same idea: a plain sentence about what went wrong.

**Mixing up the value and the position.** `shopping[1]` means "the item at position 1". `shopping.remove("bread")` means "the item whose value is bread". One is a place, the other is a thing.

## Try this yourself

Open a new file and type this out, changing the values to three places you would like to visit:

```python
trips = ["Kandy", "Lisbon", "Oslo"]
print("I have", len(trips), "trips planned")
print("First stop:", trips[0])
trips.append("Cairo")
print("Last stop is now:", trips[-1])
trips.remove("Lisbon")
print(trips)
```

Run it. Then break it on purpose: ask for `trips[9]` and read the error message it gives you. Getting comfortable with that message now will save you hours later.
learning_objectives: Create a list that holds several values in the order you put them in
Read any single value out of a list using its position, counting from zero
Change a list with append, remove and pop, and measure it with len
Recognise an IndexError and work out which position was asked for by mistake
lessons.case_study:
**The Hawaii false missile alert — the wrong item in a list (2018)**

On the morning of 13 January 2018 the Hawaii Emergency Management Agency sent an alert to mobile phones across the state: a ballistic missile was inbound, take shelter, this is not a drill. It was not true. People ran for basements, parents said goodbye to children over the phone, and the correction did not reach phones for about 38 minutes.

Inside the agency the alert had been sent from a menu — a list of alert templates on a screen. Sitting in that list, close together, were a drill template and a live template with almost the same wording. The first accounts blamed a slip of the mouse: the wrong item picked from a list. The investigation by the Federal Communications Commission, published in April 2018, found something more uncomfortable. The warning officer had heard a drill recording that itself contained the words "this is not a drill", believed a real attack was under way, and deliberately chose the live template. Either way, the software did exactly what it was told.

That is the part worth carrying into this lesson. A program that works with a list knows the position you picked. It does not know what you meant. When two items in a list look nearly identical, and when picking one of them does something that cannot be undone, the list itself has become the hazard. The FCC report criticised the lack of a second person confirming the send, and the absence of a quick way to cancel.

The fixes were unglamorous and mostly about the list: separate the drill options from the live ones, label them so they cannot be confused at a glance, and add a confirmation step before anything goes out. You will make the same class of mistake in your own code this week, at a far smaller scale — reaching for position 3 in a list that only has positions 0, 1 and 2. Same lesson, no evacuation required.

exercises.title: Reaching the first item
exercises.prompt_md: You have a list called `colours` that holds four colour names, and you want to print the very first one. Which line of code gives you that first value?
options: print(colours[0]), because list positions start counting at zero
print(colours[1]), because the first item sits at position one
print(colours(0)), because round brackets are used for positions
print(colours.first), because first is the name of the opening item
exercises.correct_answer: print(colours[0]), because list positions start counting at zero

exercises.title: What len gives back
exercises.prompt_md: You write `animals = ["cat", "dog", "fox"]` and then run `print(len(animals))`. What appears on the screen when you run the program?
options: 3, because len counts how many items the list holds
2, because len counts positions and those start at zero
fox, because len hands back the item sitting at the end
The whole list of animals, because len shows every item it holds
exercises.correct_answer: 3, because len counts how many items the list holds

exercises.title: The message for a position that is not there
exercises.prompt_md: Your list holds three items. You ask Python for the item at position 3, the program stops, and a message is printed. Which message is the one you would see?
options: IndexError: list index out of range
KeyError: 3 is not a key in this list
TypeError: list positions must be whole numbers
ValueError: 3 is not in the list you gave
exercises.correct_answer: IndexError: list index out of range

exercises.title: Why one common append line fails
exercises.prompt_md: A learner writes `scores = scores.append(10)` and afterwards their program behaves as though the list has vanished entirely. What is actually going wrong on that line?
options: append changes the list where it sits and hands back nothing, so scores now holds nothing
append needs the position you want to add at, so the line is missing an argument
append works only on lists of text, so a number is refused without warning
append builds a copy and leaves the original list untouched, so nothing is added
exercises.correct_answer: append changes the list where it sits and hands back nothing, so scores now holds nothing

exercises.title: Position or value
exercises.prompt_md: You have `shopping = ["milk", "bread", "eggs"]` and you want to take out the bread, but you do not want to think about where bread sits in the list. Which line does that?
options: shopping.remove("bread"), because remove searches for the value you name
shopping.remove(1), because remove always wants the position of the item
shopping[1] = nothing, because clearing a position deletes that item
shopping.pop("bread"), because pop takes out the value you name
exercises.correct_answer: shopping.remove("bread"), because remove searches for the value you name

exercises.title: Explain counting from zero
exercises.prompt_md: In your own words, explain to somebody who has never coded why the first item of a Python list sits at position 0, and what that means for the position number of the last item in a list of ten items.
exercises.correct_answer: Python treats a position as how many steps along from the start an item is, so the first item is zero steps along and sits at position 0. Each item after that is one more step, so the second is at 1 and the third at 2. In a list of ten items the positions run from 0 to 9, so the last item is at position 9, which is the length minus one.

exercises.title: Diagnosing an IndexError
exercises.prompt_md: A friend messages you: "My list definitely has 5 items, I checked with len. But when I ask for `items[5]` the program stops with an IndexError." Explain what has happened and what they should write instead to reach the final item.
exercises.correct_answer: Their list really does have five items, but the positions run 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, so position 5 does not exist and Python stops with an IndexError. The highest position is always the length minus one. To reach the final item they should ask for items[4], or better, items[-1], because a negative position counts back from the end and always lands on the last item.

exercises.title: When a list starts to hurt
exercises.prompt_md: A colleague stores prices as `prices = [1.20, 2.50, 3.10]` and keeps a note on paper saying that position 0 is milk, position 1 is bread and position 2 is eggs. Describe two things that are likely to go wrong with this arrangement as the program grows.
exercises.correct_answer: The meaning of each position lives outside the program, on paper, so anybody reading the code cannot tell what a price belongs to. If somebody adds, removes or reorders an item, every position shifts and the paper note is silently wrong, which gives a wrong price rather than an error. Looking up the price of bread also means remembering a number instead of the name, which gets harder as the list grows.

exercises.title: pop and remove side by side
exercises.prompt_md: Describe the difference between `queue.pop()` and `queue.remove("Ana")` for a list called queue, and give one situation where you would reach for each of them.
exercises.correct_answer: pop takes an item out by position and hands that item back to you, so you can store it in a variable; with no position given it takes the last one. remove searches for the first item whose value matches what you named and takes that out, handing nothing back. You would use pop when you want to take the next item off a queue and then work with it, and remove when you know the value that should no longer be in the list, such as a person who has cancelled.

exercises.title: Lists in the Hawaii alert
exercises.prompt_md: Thinking about the false missile alert in Hawaii, explain what it means to say that a program knows which item of a list was chosen but not what the person meant, and name one change that reduces the risk of the wrong item being picked.
exercises.correct_answer: A program receives only the position or label that was selected, so a live alert and a drill alert sitting next to each other in the same list look equally valid to it and it carries out whichever one arrives. It has no way of knowing the person intended the other one. Sensible changes include labelling items so similar options cannot be confused at a glance, keeping practice options in a separate place from real ones, and requiring a confirmation step before anything that cannot be undone.

lessons.title: Looking things up by name with dictionaries
lessons.theory_md:
## Remembering that position 7 is the butter

A list is good at order and bad at names. If you store prices as `prices = [1.20, 2.50, 3.10]`, then the fact that the middle one is bread lives nowhere in your program. It lives in your head, or on a sticky note. Add one item at the front and every position shifts by one, your sticky note is now wrong, and the program cheerfully tells a customer the wrong price. No error, no warning — a quiet wrong answer, which is the worst kind.

What you want is to look things up by **name** instead of by position. Python has a tool for exactly that, and it is called a **dictionary**, usually shortened to **dict**.

## Key and value, like a real dictionary

In a paper dictionary you look up a word and get its meaning. In a Python dictionary you look up a **key** and get its **value**. You write it with curly brackets `{ }`, a colon between each key and its value, and commas between the pairs.

```python
prices = {"milk": 1.20, "bread": 2.50, "eggs": 3.10}
print(prices["bread"])
print(len(prices))
```

Output:

```
2.5
3
```

`prices["bread"]` says "give me the value stored under the key bread". Notice the square brackets are back, but a name goes inside them now, not a position number. And notice `2.5`, not `2.50`: to Python they are the same number and it prints the shortest form. That is not an error, it is arithmetic. `len` still works and counts the pairs.

## Adding, changing and checking

```python
prices = {"milk": 1.20, "bread": 2.50}
prices["butter"] = 2.90
prices["milk"] = 1.35
print(prices)
print("jam" in prices)
print(prices.get("jam"))
print(prices.get("jam", 0))
```

Output:

```
{'milk': 1.35, 'bread': 2.5, 'butter': 2.9}
False
None
0
```

Four ideas in one small program. Assigning to a key that does not exist yet **adds** it. Assigning to a key that already exists **replaces** the old value, silently — `milk` went from 1.20 to 1.35 and nothing warned you. `in` answers a plain yes or no question and gives back `True` or `False`, the two values you met last week. And `get` is the polite way to ask: if the key is missing you get `None`, which is Python's word for "nothing here", or whatever stand-in value you name second, such as `0`.

## When the key is not there

Asking for a missing key with square brackets is not polite, and Python stops:

```python
prices = {"milk": 1.20, "bread": 2.50}
print(prices["jam"])
```

Output:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "prices.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(prices["jam"])
KeyError: 'jam'
```

`KeyError: 'jam'` means "there is no key called jam in here". It even tells you which key it could not find. Compare that with the list error from last lesson: `IndexError` is about a position, `KeyError` is about a name. When you see one, you already know which kind of thing you were searching.

## Changing a value based on the value it already has

You will do this constantly: take what is stored, change it, put it back under the same key.

```python
stock = {"milk": 2, "bread": 1}
stock["milk"] = stock["milk"] - 1
print(stock)
```

Output:

```
{'milk': 1, 'bread': 1}
```

Read the middle line from the right: `stock["milk"]` is fetched, one is taken off it, and the answer is stored back under `stock["milk"]`. The key never changes; only the value does. If that line looks odd, it is the same idea as `count = count + 1` from last week, with a dictionary entry in place of a plain variable.

## The mistakes people actually make here

**Keys must match exactly.** `prices["Milk"]` is not `prices["milk"]`. A capital letter, a trailing space, or `"1"` instead of `1` all count as different keys. Most beginner `KeyError` messages are a spelling difference, not a missing item.

**A repeated key does not raise an error.** Writing `stock = {"apples": 5, "apples": 9}` then printing gives `{'apples': 9}`. The second value wins and the first disappears without a word. A key is unique by design: one key, one value.

**Reaching for a dictionary when order is the point.** Dictionaries do keep the order you added things in, but that is not what they are for. If you are recording the finishing order of a race, a list says what you mean. If you are recording each runner's time, a dictionary says what you mean.

**Forgetting a value can itself be a list.** `basket = {"fruit": ["apple", "pear"]}` is perfectly normal, and `basket["fruit"][0]` gives `apple`: look up the key, then take position 0 of the list you got back.

## So when does a dict beat a list?

Ask one question: *do I find things by where they are, or by what they are called?* Positions in a queue, steps in a recipe, scores in the order they happened — list. Prices by product, phone numbers by person, settings by name — dictionary. If you ever catch yourself writing a comment that says "position 2 is the postcode", you wanted a dictionary.

## Try this yourself

```python
me = {"name": "Sam", "town": "Galle", "cats": 2}
print("Name:", me["name"])
me["cats"] = me["cats"] + 1
print("Cats now:", me["cats"])
me["job"] = "learning to code"
print(me)
print("age" in me)
print(me.get("age", "not saying"))
```

Run it with your own details. Then ask for `me["age"]` with square brackets and read the `KeyError` it gives you — knowing what that message looks like when you caused it deliberately makes it far less frightening when you have not.
learning_objectives: Create a dictionary that pairs each key with a value
Look up, add and change values using their key rather than a position
Handle a missing key safely using get and the word in, and read a KeyError
Decide whether a list or a dictionary fits a given piece of information
lessons.case_study:
**Microsoft Excel and the gene names it turned into dates (2016-2020)**

Human genes have short names. One family was called SEPT1, SEPT2 and so on; another MARCH1, MARCH2. Type `SEPT2` into a spreadsheet cell in Microsoft Excel with the usual settings and the program helpfully decides you meant a date and stores 2-Sep instead. The scientist does not notice, because the file looks fine, and the name is now something else forever.

In 2016 Mark Ziemann, Yotam Eren and Assam El-Osta published a study in Genome Biology examining supplementary gene lists attached to papers across eighteen journals. They reported that roughly one in five of the papers they checked contained gene names mangled this way. The data had not been lost or corrupted in any dramatic sense. It had been silently renamed, and every later attempt to look those genes up by name would miss them.

What makes this a story about dictionaries rather than about spreadsheets is where the damage lands. Looking something up by name only works if the name is exactly the name. Change one character and the lookup does not return a wrong answer with a warning attached; it returns nothing, or it quietly matches something else. In 2020 the body responsible for naming human genes gave up on fixing the software and changed the data instead, renaming the affected genes so autocorrect would leave them alone: SEPT1 became SEPTIN1, MARCH1 became MARCHF1.

It did not settle the matter. A follow-up study by Abeysooriya and colleagues, published in PLOS Computational Biology in 2021, looked at a much larger set of papers and found the proportion carrying mangled gene names had gone up rather than down. When you write `prices["milk"]` this week and get a KeyError because you typed `Milk`, you are meeting the same rule that cost genetics researchers years of quiet errors: a key is only a key if it matches exactly.

exercises.title: Getting a value out of a dictionary
exercises.prompt_md: You have `ages = {"Ana": 31, "Bo": 24}` and you want to print the number stored for Bo. Which line of code gives you that value?
options: print(ages["Bo"]), because a value is fetched using its key in square brackets
print(ages[1]), because Bo is the second pair that was added to the dictionary
print(ages.Bo), because a key is reached by writing it after a full stop
print(ages("Bo")), because round brackets are used for looking up a key
exercises.correct_answer: print(ages["Bo"]), because a value is fetched using its key in square brackets

exercises.title: Assigning to a key that is missing
exercises.prompt_md: Your dictionary `prices` holds keys for milk and bread only, and you run the line `prices["butter"] = 2.90`. What does Python do when that line runs?
options: It adds a new pair, so the dictionary now holds a key called butter with the value 2.9
It stops with a KeyError, because butter has to exist before it can be given a value
It replaces the whole dictionary with a single pair for butter, losing the others
It does nothing at all, because a dictionary cannot grow after it has been made
exercises.correct_answer: It adds a new pair, so the dictionary now holds a key called butter with the value 2.9

exercises.title: Reading a KeyError
exercises.prompt_md: A program stops and the final line of the message reads `KeyError: 'jam'`. Which of these is the most reliable description of what has happened in the program?
options: The dictionary has no key called jam, so there is no value to hand back
The value stored under jam is empty, so Python refuses to print it
The key jam appears twice in the dictionary, so Python cannot choose
The key jam was given a number when the dictionary expected text
exercises.correct_answer: The dictionary has no key called jam, so there is no value to hand back

exercises.title: The polite way to ask
exercises.prompt_md: You are not sure whether the key `"jam"` exists in a dictionary called prices, and you want your program to carry on regardless rather than stopping. Which line is the safe way to ask for it?
options: prices.get("jam", 0), because get hands back a stand-in value when the key is absent
prices["jam"], because square brackets return an empty value for a missing key
prices.remove("jam"), because removing a missing key leaves the dictionary as it was
prices.append("jam"), because append checks first and only adds what is missing
exercises.correct_answer: prices.get("jam", 0), because get hands back a stand-in value when the key is absent

exercises.title: Choosing between a list and a dictionary
exercises.prompt_md: You need to store the mobile number of each person in a club, and your program will always start from a person and need their number. Which storage choice fits the job and why?
options: A dictionary, because you look each number up by the name it belongs to
A list of numbers, because a list is faster than a dictionary for any job
A list of numbers, because the position of a person never changes over time
A dictionary, because it keeps the numbers sorted from smallest to largest
exercises.correct_answer: A dictionary, because you look each number up by the name it belongs to

exercises.title: Explain a key and a value
exercises.prompt_md: Explain the words key and value to someone who has never programmed, using an example from everyday life rather than from code, and say what makes a key different from a position in a list.
exercises.correct_answer: A key is the label you search under and the value is what you get back, exactly like a phone contacts app where you search a name and get a number. The key has to be unique, so one key holds one value, and looking up the key is how you reach that value. A position in a list only tells you where something sits in an order, so it changes if the order changes, whereas a key stays meaningful no matter what else is added or removed.

exercises.title: The silent overwrite
exercises.prompt_md: A learner writes `stock = {"apples": 5, "apples": 9}` and then prints stock, which shows `{'apples': 9}`. Explain why no error appeared and why this behaviour is worth being careful about.
exercises.correct_answer: A dictionary allows one value per key, so the second apples pair replaced the first as the dictionary was built and Python saw nothing wrong with that. No error appears because overwriting a key is a normal, deliberate feature, used every time you update a value. It is worth care because a duplicated or accidentally reused key loses data quietly, and the program then runs to completion giving a wrong answer rather than stopping with a message you could read.

exercises.title: Two errors, two shapes of question
exercises.prompt_md: Explain the difference between an IndexError and a KeyError in terms of what you were asking Python for in each case, and say what each message tells you about where to look in your code.
exercises.correct_answer: An IndexError comes from a list and means you asked for a position that does not exist, so you should check the length of the list and remember the highest position is the length minus one. A KeyError comes from a dictionary and means you asked for a name that is not among the keys, so you should check the spelling, capital letters and spaces of the key. In short, one is a complaint about a place and the other is a complaint about a name, which tells you immediately which kind of collection to inspect.

exercises.title: Applying the gene name lesson
exercises.prompt_md: Using the gene names story, explain in your own words why a key that is very slightly altered is more dangerous than a key that is plainly absent, and suggest one habit that reduces the risk in your own programs.
exercises.correct_answer: A key that is plainly absent usually produces a KeyError, which stops the program and points straight at the problem, so it gets fixed quickly. A key that has been slightly altered, such as SEPT2 becoming a date or milk becoming Milk, may still match nothing or match the wrong entry while looking perfectly normal to a human reader, so the wrong result flows on unnoticed. A helpful habit is to decide one exact form for every key, for example all lower case with no spaces, and to tidy any text into that form before using it as a key.

exercises.title: Redesign a fragile store
exercises.prompt_md: A program stores a customer record as the list `["Ana Perera", "Galle", 31, "ana@example.com"]` and other code reaches into it by position. Describe how you would store the same record as a dictionary and what improves as a result.
exercises.correct_answer: I would store it as a dictionary such as name, town, age and email as keys with those four values, so each piece of information carries its own label. Code elsewhere then asks for record with the key name or the key email instead of remembering that position 3 is the address. Nothing breaks when a new field is added or the order changes, and anyone reading the code can see what each value means without a separate note.

lessons.title: Doing something to every item with loops
lessons.theory_md:
## The copy and paste smell

Here is a program that says hello to three people.

```python
print("Hello, Ana")
print("Hello, Bo")
print("Hello, Cy")
```

It works. Now do it for three hundred people. You cannot, and you should not want to. Whenever you find yourself copying a line and changing one small part of it, the language is trying to tell you something: this is a job for a **loop**.

A loop is an instruction that says "do this again, for each of these". It is the single biggest jump in power you will make in this course.

## A for loop over a list

```python
names = ["Ana", "Bo", "Cy"]
for name in names:
    print("Hello,", name)
print("Finished")
```

Output:

```
Hello, Ana
Hello, Bo
Hello, Cy
Finished
```

Read the loop line out loud as English: "for each name in names". Python takes the first item, puts it in the variable `name`, runs the indented line, then comes back for the next item, and stops when the list runs out.

Two details matter enormously. The colon at the end of the `for` line, and the **indentation** — the spaces at the start of the next line. Those spaces are what tell Python which lines belong to the loop. `print("Finished")` is not indented, so it sits outside and runs once at the end. If you indented it, it would run three times. Use four spaces, and be consistent; Python will stop with `IndentationError` if you are careless, which is a kindness.

The word `name` is your choice. `for x in names` works identically. Pick a word that says what one item is.

## A for loop over a dictionary

A dictionary has two things per entry, so you ask for both:

```python
stock = {"milk": 2, "bread": 1, "eggs": 6}
total = 0
for product, count in stock.items():
    print(product, "-", count)
    total = total + count
print("Total items:", total)
```

Output:

```
milk - 2
bread - 1
eggs - 6
Total items: 9
```

`stock.items()` hands the loop each pair, so `product` gets the key and `count` gets the value. The `total` variable is a **running total**: it starts at zero outside the loop, and each pass adds to it. Starting it outside is essential. Move `total = 0` inside the loop and it resets on every pass, so you finish with only the last number.

## Counting with range

Sometimes you want to repeat something a fixed number of times rather than walk a list.

```python
for number in range(3):
    print(number)
```

Output:

```
0
1
2
```

`range(3)` gives three numbers starting at zero: 0, 1, 2. It stops **before** 3. This is the same counting-from-zero idea as list positions, and it is the source of the most famous beginner bug of all, the **off-by-one**: `range(1, 4)` gives 1, 2, 3, while `range(1, 3)` gives only 1 and 2. When a loop does one pass too many or too few, look here first.

## The loop that never ends

There is a second kind of loop, `while`, which repeats for as long as something stays true. It is where beginners get burned.

```python
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("Lift off")
```

Output:

```
3
2
1
Lift off
```

That works because `count` gets smaller each pass, so the test eventually becomes false. Now delete one level of indentation from `count = count - 1` so it sits outside the loop. The test is `3 > 0` forever, and the program prints `3` down the screen until you stop it. That is an **infinite loop**. Nothing is broken, your computer is fine, and you stop it by pressing **Ctrl and C** together in the window where it is running.

The rule: every `while` loop must contain something that eventually makes its test false. If you cannot point at that line, you have written an infinite loop.

## The mistakes people actually make here

**Changing a list while looping over it.** This one gives no error and a wrong answer:

```python
names = ["ana", "ana", "bo"]
for name in names:
    if name == "ana":
        names.remove(name)
print(names)
```

Output:

```
['ana', 'bo']
```

One `ana` survived. Removing an item shifted everything left while the loop was still counting forwards, so the loop skipped over an item. Never add to or remove from a list you are currently looping over. Build a new list instead:

```python
names = ["ana", "ana", "bo"]
kept = []
for name in names:
    if name != "ana":
        kept.append(name)
print(kept)
```

Output: `['bo']`. Predictable, boring, correct.

**Forgetting the indentation.** Everything the loop should repeat must be indented under it.

**Looping over the wrong thing.** `for letter in "milk"` loops over the four letters, not over one word. If your loop prints single characters, that is why.

## Try this yourself

```python
prices = {"milk": 120, "bread": 250, "eggs": 310}
total = 0
for product, pence in prices.items():
    print(product, "costs", pence, "pence")
    total = total + pence
print("Basket total in pence:", total)
```

Run it, then add a fourth product and run it again without changing anything else. That is the payoff: the loop did not need to know how many products there were. Then write a `while` loop that counts down from 5, run it, and deliberately remove the line that changes the counter so you can watch an infinite loop and stop it with Ctrl and C. Doing that once on purpose is worth more than reading about it ten times.

Loop over a dictionary and build a running total from its values
Use range to repeat something a fixed number of times without an off-by-one mistake
Spot and avoid infinite loops and changes made to a list while looping over it
lessons.case_study:
**Microsoft Zune — the players that froze on the last day of 2008 (2008)**

On 31 December 2008, thousands of Microsoft Zune 30 music players stopped working at once. Owners woke to a device that switched on, showed the loading screen, and stayed there. It was not a virus and not a battery fault, and it hit every unit of that model on the same day, worldwide.

The cause was a loop. Deep in the player, a piece of clock code kept the date by counting days since 1980 and then converting that count into a year. The code worked like this: while there are more than 365 days left, if this is a leap year and there are more than 366 days left, take 366 off and move to the next year; otherwise take 365 off and move on. Read it slowly with the number 366 in your hand, on the last day of the leap year 2008. There are more than 365 days left, so the loop runs. It is a leap year, but there are not more than 366 days left. So nothing is subtracted, nothing moves, and the loop asks the same question again. And again. The device was not frozen in the sense of being stuck doing nothing; it was working extremely hard, forever, on a question that could no longer change.

The code in question came from a driver written for a part used only in that model, which is why the newer Zunes were unaffected. Microsoft's advice to owners was almost comic and entirely correct: let the battery run flat, then charge the player up again after midday GMT on 1 January. Once the calendar moved on, the day count was 1, the loop condition was false, and every affected device recovered by itself.

This is the exact trap in the `while` loop section above, at industrial scale, written by professionals. It is worth being clear about what that means: an infinite loop is not a beginner mistake you will grow out of. It is a permanent hazard of the tool, and the defence is always the same one you are learning now. Before you run a while loop, find the line that eventually makes the test false, and check that it really runs on every path through the loop.

exercises.title: How many times the loop runs
exercises.prompt_md: You write `for item in ["a", "b", "c", "d"]:` with one indented print line underneath it. How many times does that indented line run when the program is started?
options: Four times, once for each item that the list holds
Three times, because the loop stops before the final item
Once, because the whole list is handed over in a single pass
Five times, because the loop also runs once for the empty end
exercises.correct_answer: Four times, once for each item that the list holds

exercises.title: What range gives you
exercises.prompt_md: A learner writes `for number in range(3):` and prints number each time round the loop. Which numbers appear on the screen, in the order they are printed?
options: 0, then 1, then 2, because range starts at zero and stops before three
1, then 2, then 3, because range counts up to the number you gave it
0, then 1, then 2, then 3, because both ends are included in the count
3, then 2, then 1, because range counts down towards zero by default
exercises.correct_answer: 0, then 1, then 2, because range starts at zero and stops before three

exercises.title: Where the running total belongs
exercises.prompt_md: A program adds up numbers in a loop, but it always reports the final number instead of the sum of all of them. Where has the line `total = 0` most likely been placed by mistake?
options: Inside the loop, so the total is reset to zero on every single pass
Before the list is created, so the total is emptied when the list is made
After the loop, so the total is wiped once all the adding has finished
In the loop condition, so the total is compared rather than stored
exercises.correct_answer: Inside the loop, so the total is reset to zero on every single pass

exercises.title: Recognising an infinite loop
exercises.prompt_md: A while loop keeps printing the same value down the screen and never reaches the line after it. Which explanation describes what has gone wrong inside that loop?
options: Nothing inside the loop changes the value being tested, so the test stays true forever
The loop has too many indented lines, so Python cannot decide when to leave it
The computer has run out of memory, so it repeats the last line it managed to finish
The list being looped over is too long, so the loop restarts itself from the beginning
exercises.correct_answer: Nothing inside the loop changes the value being tested, so the test stays true forever

exercises.title: Looping over a dictionary
exercises.prompt_md: You have a dictionary called `stock` and you want a loop that gives you the key and the value together on each pass. Which loop line does that?
options: for product, count in stock.items():
for product in stock.keys():
for count in stock.values():
for product, count in stock:
exercises.correct_answer: for product, count in stock.items():

exercises.title: Explain indentation to a beginner
exercises.prompt_md: Explain in your own words what the indented spaces underneath a for loop line are for, and describe what changes if a print line that should be inside the loop is written without indentation.
exercises.correct_answer: The indentation marks which lines belong to the loop, so everything indented under the for line is repeated once for each item. Python uses those spaces instead of any other marker, which is why they are not optional. If a print line that belongs inside the loop is written without indentation it sits outside the loop, so it runs once after the loop has finished rather than once per item, and the output is much shorter than expected.

exercises.title: The Zune loop in your own words
exercises.prompt_md: Using the Zune story, explain what an infinite loop is and describe the one check you should carry out on every while loop you write before you run it.
exercises.correct_answer: An infinite loop is a loop whose test never becomes false, so the instructions inside it repeat for as long as the program is allowed to run and the lines after the loop are never reached. In the Zune case the day count sat at a value where neither branch subtracted anything, so the same question was asked forever and the player never finished starting up. Before running any while loop I should find the line inside it that moves the tested value towards making the test false, and check that this line actually runs on every path through the loop.

exercises.title: Why removing while looping goes wrong
exercises.prompt_md: A learner loops over a list and removes matching items as they go, and afterwards some matching items are still there. Explain why that happens and describe the safer approach.
exercises.correct_answer: The loop walks forwards through the positions of the list, but removing an item shifts every later item one place to the left, so the next item slides into a position the loop has already passed and is skipped. No error appears because nothing illegal happened, which is why the result is a quietly wrong list. The safer approach is to leave the original list alone and build a new empty list, appending only the items you want to keep, then use that new list afterwards.

exercises.title: Chasing an off-by-one
exercises.prompt_md: A program is meant to print the numbers 1 to 10 but prints 1 to 9. The loop line reads `for n in range(1, 10):`. Explain what is happening and how you would fix it.
exercises.correct_answer: range stops before the second number it is given, so range(1, 10) produces 1 up to 9 and never includes 10. That is the off-by-one mistake: the loop runs one pass fewer than intended. The fix is to write range(1, 11), which produces 1 to 10, and the general habit is to remember that the second number is where the counting stops rather than the last value you get.

exercises.title: Choosing between for and while
exercises.prompt_md: Describe when you would reach for a for loop and when a while loop suits the job better, and say which of the two is more likely to run forever and why.
exercises.correct_answer: A for loop suits work where you already know what you are stepping through, such as every item in a list or a fixed number of repeats with range, because it ends by itself when it runs out of items. A while loop suits work that carries on until some condition changes, such as repeating until a total is reached, because the number of passes is not known in advance. The while loop is the one that can run forever, since nothing stops it automatically and it depends on you changing the value it tests.
